Guisers! Masked and blacked like the old ones, so the wandering dead won't know you. Here's nuts for the fire.

You're going up to Ravensmoor, aren't you? Everyone does. Count the rooms. If you count fourteen, run.
Soul, soul, a soul cake! I pray you, good missus, a soul cake!
The night is dark, the moon is high, give us a treat or we'll pass you by!
Here we come a-guising, masked so the dead won't know: a nut, an apple, a soul cake, and away we go!
The two nuts burn together, quiet and steady: a true friend sits beside you all year.
Your nut cracks and jumps from the fire! A restless year: you will travel far.
The nut burns slow and bright: good luck finds you before the snow.
It flares and is gone: a short sharp trouble, then joy.
Silas Ravensmoor laid a supper for the dead on Samhain, 1789, and locked the doors so they could not leave. They never have.
The corridor is longer every time you walk it.
Edgar Allan Poe, The Raven (1845): 'Once upon a midnight dreary'. A raven sits on the bust over the door.
Charlotte Perkins Gilman, The Yellow Wallpaper (1892): a woman creeps behind the pattern.
Something still plays in the nursery.
The Dumb Supper, an old Samhain custom: a meal laid in silence for the dead, a chair for each.
In one of the mirrors your reflection does not do what you do.
Poe, The Tell-Tale Heart (1843): 'It is the beating of his hideous heart!' under the boards.
The Bell Board and the Servants' Stair
The bells ring for rooms that are not in the house.
Poe, The Cask of Amontillado (1846): a niche bricked up, and a jingle of bells behind it.
Under the chapel, the Ravensmoors sleep. Mostly.
The Seven Chambers
Poe, The Masque of the Red Death (1842): seven rooms, blue, purple, green, orange, white, violet and black, and the ebony clock.
The Grey Lady keens in the attic, the bean sidhe of the Ravensmoors. Ring the tower bell and the house lets you go.

A villager of Hollowmere on Samhain night, 1820s Ireland: talks of the fire on the Hill of Tlachtga, guising, soul cakes, the Dumb Supper, the Dullahan who rides the road from the mill, and Ravensmoor House up the hill that no one goes near. Speaks plainly, warmly, a little afraid.
Samhain night, the night the door between the worlds stands open. Mind yourself.

The cheerful keeper of Pumpkin Hollow, for children: tells about the candy trail (13 sweets), the hay maze and its corn dolly, carving pumpkins, the five friendly ghosts in the Giggling House and the films in the Pumpkin Playhouse. Kind, bright, never scary. Explains that long ago in Ireland people carved turnips, and pumpkins came later in America.

👥 Every chair is taken. Dark guests sit in silence, heads bowed over their plates. Not one of them breathes. The far door stands open.
🪞 In the middle mirror, the one who is not you smiles , and lifts a hand, and beckons. The glass is cold as water. You can step through it (the far door).

❤️ Under the board, wrapped in sacking, something still beats. Once, very loudly. Then never again. 'Villains! dissemble no more! I admit the deed! tear up the planks! here, here! It is the beating of his hideous heart!'
🪵 Dust and old nails. The beating is louder somewhere else .
Listen. Follow the beating heart, and lift the board it is under.

🃏 The bricks come away. In the niche, chained to the wall, sits a skeleton in a jester's cap of bells. Under it, scratched in the stone: 'For the love of God, Montresor!' And then, as Poe wrote: 'In pace requiescat!'
Listen for the bells in the wall.
⚰️ Stone grinds on stone. Beside you, a coffin lid is sliding open , from the inside.
Light the candles on the altar.
Reach the ebony clock in the black room, and stop it before the hour strikes.
🕰️ The Seven Chambers. Far ahead, in the black room, the ebony clock ticks. When it strikes the hour, the dancers freeze, and something masked walks among them . You have about a minute.
🕰️ You catch the great brass pendulum. The clock stops, one tick before the hour. In the scarlet light, all through the seven rooms, the dancers turn their heads to look at you.
🎭 The clock strikes. A tall figure in a shroud, masked like a corpse, stands right in front of you. 'And Darkness and Decay and the Red Death held illimitable dominion over all.'
🔵 You are back in the blue room. The clock ticks again. Run.
🔔 BONG. Over your head the great bell of Ravensmoor tolls, and tolls, and tolls. The Grey Lady's keening breaks off. The roof hatch at the end swings open on the storm.
Ring the bell. The rope hangs at the far end.

You've guised at every door in Hollowmere!
On Samhain night children went door to door in masks and blackened faces (so the wandering dead would not know them), and sang or said a rhyme for a soul cake, nuts or apples.
🌰 You set two hazelnuts side by side on the hearth, one for you, one for someone you're thinking of, as they did on Snap-Apple Night.
🍎 Bobbing for apples
Hands behind your back! Bite when the apple floats into the gap.
🍎 Got it! You come up soaked to the ears, a red apple in your teeth. They say if you sleep with it under your pillow, you'll dream of your true love.
💦 Only a mouthful of cold water. Try again!
🏮 Light my turnip lantern from the fire
💬 Talk with the fire keeper
🔥 The fire keeper of Tlachtga
On Samhain every hearth in the land was put out, and lit again from the great fire on the Hill of Tlachtga.
Samhain (say it SOW-in) is the old Gaelic feast at the end of harvest, from sunset on 31 October: the night the door between this world and the Otherworld stands open.
People left food out for the dead, laid a Dumb Supper in silence, and went guising in masks so the wandering spirits would pass them by.

Stingy Jack, they say, tricked the Devil and was turned away from heaven and hell both, with one ember of hellfire in a turnip to light his way. His lantern went into the ground with the Ravensmoors, under their chapel, 'behind the eyes of the dead'.
Halloween's pumpkins came later, in America, where pumpkins were easier to carve than turnips.
The fire keeper of Tlachtga
Sit by the fire a while, traveller. The dead are walking tonight.
🏮 Your turnip lantern is already burning with the Samhain fire.
🏮 You hold your carved turnip to the great fire, and it takes the flame. Your lantern burns with the Samhain fire : it lights your way all night, and the dead let it pass.
🐴 Hoofbeats, behind you. A great black horse, and on it a rider with no head, his own head blazing in his hand. Run for the church bridge! He cannot cross the water.
🎃 You're over the bridge! The Horseman rears at the water's edge, and hurls his blazing head. It smashes on the boards behind you: only a pumpkin. When you look back, horse and rider are gone.
💥 The blazing head strikes you. You wake in the road by the old mill, your hat gone, and a smashed pumpkin beside you. Try again: run straight for the church bridge.
🌫️ The hoofbeats fade into the mist. He'll ride again.
🔒 Ravensmoor House is shut for now, by the Keeper.
Thirteen rooms. The freakiest house in Samhain Night.
13 and up. It is very frightening: real darkness, sudden noises, lightning, things that follow you and things that chase you. (No strobe.)
Carry your candle through every room. Each far door opens only when you've done what that room asks. From the Nursery on, the Grey Lady hunts you: run for the next door, or hide in a wardrobe.
Pumpkin Hollow, east of the village, is bright and friendly.
🔔 A bell is ringing on the board: the one marked The Fourteenth Room . Ravensmoor has thirteen.
